result: Hippocampome.org v1.0 established a foundational classification system for 122 hippocampal neuron types based on axonal and dendritic morphologies, neurotransmitter type, membrane biophysics, and molecular expression. This morphology-based approach provides advantages including revealing circuit connectivity, serving as an anchoring signature for correlating other properties, and avoiding inconsistent nomenclature.
evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C10 collectively establish the foundational classification system and its rationale. The claims are well-supported by citations to the original publication (Wheeler et al., 2015) and supporting literature (Rees et al., 2017; DeFelipe et al., 2013). The classification framework is clearly described and justified.

result: Hippocampome.org releases v1.1 through v1.12 progressively expanded the knowledge base over 100-fold by adding diverse neuronal properties including: terminology mapping (v1.1), connectivity analysis (v1.2), transcriptomic data (v1.3, v1.5), firing patterns and Izhikevich models (v1.6, v1.7), in vivo recordings (v1.9), cognitive functions (v1.10), neuron census (v1.11), and synaptic physiology with normalized parameters (v1.4, v1.8, v1.12).
evaluation: Claims C2, C11-C21 describe the progressive expansion of the database across versions. Each version's contribution is supported by specific citations to peer-reviewed publications. The 100-fold increase claim (C2) is supported by the description of accumulated data, particularly the 500,000 pieces of knowledge from synaptic properties (C109, C110). The claims are internally consistent and well-documented.

result: Hippocampome.org v2.0 expanded the catalog with 56 new neuron types across 5 of 6 hippocampal subregions, including morphological patterns, molecular expression, and membrane biophysics. An example is the DG Basket GRALDEN cell, identified based on specific morphological and molecular characteristics, which enabled attribution of previously reported electrophysiological properties.
evaluation: Claims C3, C22, C107, C108 describe the expansion of neuron types in v2.0. The claims are supported by Figure 2 showing the 56 new types and Figure 1B illustrating the DG Basket GRALDEN example with citations to Vaden et al., 2020 and Markwardt et al., 2011. The methodology for identifying and characterizing new types is clearly demonstrated.

result: Hippocampome.org v2.0 incorporates updated connectivity and functional distinctions for existing neuron types, including: expanded axonal projections of EC Layer III Pyramidal cells to all CA1 layers, distinction between Superficial and Deep CA1 Pyramidal cells based on in vivo firing phases and differential connectivity patterns with CA2 and PV+ interneurons.
evaluation: Claims C23-C28 describe refinements to existing neuron type characterizations. Each claim is supported by specific citations (Deller et al., 1996; Takács et al., 2012; Sanchez-Aguilera et al., 2021; Kohara et al., 2014; Valero et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2014). The claims demonstrate how the database evolves with new evidence and are illustrated in Figure 3.

result: Hippocampome.org provides four essential quantities for data-driven circuit modeling: (i) neuron counts per type derived through literature mining and numerical optimization (v1.11), (ii) input-output response functions as Izhikevich models fitted by evolutionary algorithms (v1.7), (iii) connection probabilities computed from axonal-dendritic length measurements (v1.8), and (iv) synaptic signals represented by Tsodyks-Pawelzik-Markram parameters fitted using deep learning to account for experimental variables (v1.12).
evaluation: Claims C35-C41 describe the complete framework for computational modeling. Each component is supported by citations to methods papers (Bahmer et al., 2023; DePasquale et al., 2023; Attili et al., 2020; Venkadesh et al., 2018; Tsodyks et al., 1998; Moradi et al., 2022; Cutsuridis et al., 2018) and illustrated in Figure 5. The claims provide a coherent description of the modeling pipeline.

result: Hippocampome.org integrates with external community resources including: NeuroMorpho.Org for 3D morphological reconstructions and axonal/dendritic length data, ModelDB for computational models with bidirectional linking of Izhikevich models, CARLsim for GPU-optimized simulation export, and Allen Brain Atlas for gene expression and cell density data.
evaluation: Claims C42-C47 describe integration with external resources. Each integration is supported by citations (Ascoli et al., 2007; McDougal et al., 2017; Nageswaran et al., 2009; Lein et al., 2007) and illustrated in Figure 6B. The bidirectional nature of some integrations (e.g., ModelDB) demonstrates meaningful interoperability.

result: Hippocampome.org v2.0 includes a new graphical user interface enabling users to download simulation parameters for selected neuron types, subregions, or the whole hippocampal formation. The system includes an importance ranking (1-5) for neuron types and provides default values for missing parameters, including precomputed connection-type-specific synaptic probabilities.
evaluation: Claims C48-C51 describe the new GUI functionality. The claims are clearly stated and illustrated in Figure 7. The handling of missing data with documented defaults (C50, C51) demonstrates methodological rigor. The specific default probability values are provided.

result: A real-scale mouse model of CA3 including Pyramidal cells and seven inhibitory interneuron types was constructed using Hippocampome.org parameters for cell census, Izhikevich models, synaptic signals, and connection probabilities, resulting in robust, realistic, rhythmic resting state activity for all neuron types.
evaluation: Claims C52-C54 describe an application of the resource. The work is supported by citation to Kopsick et al., 2023 and illustrated in Figure 9A. The claim that the model produces 'robust, realistic, rhythmic' activity is supported by the figure showing theta, gamma, and sharp-wave ripple oscillations. This demonstrates the utility of the compiled parameters.

result: A spiking neural network model of grid cells using Hippocampome.org Medial Entorhinal Cortex Layer II Stellate cells and supporting interneuron types implements the continuous attractor model and generates grid field activity highly compatible with that measured in behaving animals.
evaluation: Claims C55-C56 describe preliminary work on grid cell modeling. While C55 is supported by citations (Sargolini et al., 2006; Dhillon and Jones, 2000), C56 explicitly states the work is 'in preparation for publication' and represents preliminary findings. The compatibility with experimental data is claimed but not yet peer-reviewed. The result requires validation through publication.

result: Hippocampome.org has achieved substantial community impact with over 136,000 site visits including over 33,000 unique visits, and the original publication has been cited more than 100 times. Year 2021 was the most prolific for citations, though more than a third of releases (v1.8-12) appeared after 2021 with most pieces of knowledge added in 2022.
evaluation: Claims C29, C30, C63, C64, C111, C112 provide usage statistics. The claims are internally consistent (C29/C63 and C30/C64 are duplicates). The statistics are presented as direct observations and illustrated in Figure 4B. The temporal analysis noting that most recent releases occurred after peak citation year suggests potential for future growth.

result: Independent researchers have utilized Hippocampome.org data for diverse applications. Gulyás et al., 2016 used subthreshold biophysical measures for multicompartmental models, concluding that somatic recordings miss substantial synaptic inputs. Schumm et al., 2022 used the resource to model traumatic brain injury effects on hippocampal oscillations and coherence.
evaluation: Claims C31-C34 describe independent usage of the resource. Both examples are supported by specific citations (Gulyás et al., 2016; Schumm et al., 2022) and summarized in Table 3. These demonstrate real-world utility of the compiled data for addressing diverse research questions.

result: Connection probabilities and contact numbers for DG Granule cell to CA3 targets and CA3/CA3c Pyramidal cells to CA1 targets were computed using previously published anatomical measurements, morphological reconstructions, and convex hull volumes. The DG-CA3 calculations assume Granule cells only innervate stratum lucidum due to lack of information on stratum pyramidale innervation proportions.
evaluation: Claims C90-C95 describe the methodology for computing connectivity parameters. The methods are supported by multiple citations (Tecuatl et al., 2021b; Acsády et al., 1998; Ropireddy et al., 2011; Sik et al., 1993; Wittner et al., 2007; Li et al., 1994; Scorcioni et al., 2008; Winnubst et al., 2019). The explicit statement of the assumption in C91 demonstrates methodological transparency. The results are presented in Table 2 and Figure 3D.

result: Hippocampome.org has established itself among prominent bioscience resources like FlyBase, WormBase, Blue Brain Project, SynGO, and RegenBase. It has evolved from an information repository (v1.0-1.12) to a simulation platform (v2.0), distinguishing itself through exclusive reliance on published data and focused coverage of the hippocampal formation.
evaluation: Claims C57-C60 position the resource within the broader landscape. The comparisons are supported by citations to comparable resources (The FlyBase Consortium, 1994; dos Santos et al., 2015; Stein et al., 2001; Markram, 2006; Koopmans et al., 2019; Callahan et al., 2016). The distinguishing features (published data reliance, focused scope) are clearly stated.

result: While Hippocampome.org is founded on published literature data, some simulation-ready parameters result from modeling (Izhikevich and Tsodyks-Pawelzik-Markram models) or specific analysis approaches (connection probabilities from axonal-dendritic overlaps, neuron census from numerical optimization).
evaluation: Claims C61-C62 acknowledge the distinction between direct data and derived parameters. The claims are supported by citations to the modeling frameworks (Izhikevich, 2003; Tsodyks et al., 1998). This transparency about methodology strengthens the resource's credibility.

result: Future applications of Hippocampome.org include shifting focus from development to exploitation through in silico emulation of complex dynamics. Potential applications include real-scale models for studying epileptogenesis in dentate gyrus, theta oscillations in CA1, and social memory mechanisms in entorhinal cortex and CA2. Open source sharing will facilitate community understanding of neuron type roles.
evaluation: Claims C65-C70 describe future directions and potential applications. While supported by relevant citations (Sutton and Ascoli, 2021; Dyhrfjeld-Johnsen et al., 2007; Bezaire et al., 2016; Navas-Olive et al., 2020; Romani et al., 2023; Lopez-Rojas et al., 2022; Gleeson et al., 2017), these are speculative statements about future work rather than demonstrated results. The applications are plausible but not yet realized.

result: Hippocampome.org provides direct links from model parameters to peer-reviewed evidence, allowing users to evaluate and select information sources. Users can reuse experimental data to constrain alternative computational models. The resource also facilitates identification of knowledge gaps to guide future experiments and hypothesis generation.
evaluation: Claims C71-C75 describe key features enabling user control and flexibility. These are direct statements about the resource's design and functionality. The traceability to evidence (C71) is a fundamental feature demonstrated throughout. The flexibility for alternative models (C73) and gap identification (C74-C75) are logical consequences of the design.

result: Hippocampome.org carefully annotates experimental metadata including species, sex, age, and recording conditions for each piece of evidence. This enables accounting for covariates in analyses and simulations, and provides a resource for comparing and translating parameters across different experimental conditions.
evaluation: Claims C76-C78 describe metadata annotation and its utility. These are direct statements about database design and functionality. The specific example of translating parameters between conditions (C78) demonstrates practical utility. This feature is particularly important for the normalized synaptic parameters described in C21, C41.

result: Hippocampome.org is positioned to integrate emerging data from big science projects. While morphological identification will remain fundamental, the resource will link to rapidly accumulating molecular and imaging data. Future integration targets include spatial transcriptomics, single-cell RNA sequencing for transcription factor codes, genetically encoded voltage indicators for in vivo firing patterns, and computational models bridging molecular and functional data.
evaluation: Claims C79-C84 describe future integration with emerging technologies. While supported by relevant citations (de la Prida and Ascoli, 2021; Lein et al., 2017; Yao et al., 2021; Zeisel et al., 2015; Cembrowski and Spruston, 2019; Winnubst et al., 2020; Yuste et al., 2020; Knöpfel and Song, 2019; Adam et al., 2019; Migliore et al., 2018), these are forward-looking statements about potential rather than demonstrated capabilities. The integration strategies are plausible but speculative.

result: With v2.0 release, v1.12 transitions to legacy status. Hippocampome.org neuron types are linked to NeuroMorpho.Org reconstructions based on correspondence of dendritic and axonal locations. Reconstructions are excluded if experimental conditions are inconsistent with inclusion criteria (e.g., cell cultures, embryonic development) or if axonal or dendritic tracing is incomplete for non-canonical neurons.
evaluation: Claims C85-C89 describe versioning policy and linking methodology. These are direct statements of procedures supported by citation to Ascoli et al., 2007. The exclusion criteria (C88-C89) demonstrate quality control in linking morphological data.

result: Hippocampome.org utilizes CARLsim as its default simulation environment. CARLsim is a GPU-accelerated library for simulating spiking neural networks based on Izhikevich models. It was selected for its ability to run on GPU collections, necessary for simulating millions of neurons in full-scale hippocampal formation models. The current version is CARLsim 6.
evaluation: Claims C96-C99 describe the simulation environment. The claims are supported by citations (Nageswaran et al., 2009; Izhikevich, 2003; Niedermeier et al., 2022; Kopsick et al., 2023). The rationale for selection (C98) is clearly stated and logical given the scale of the models.

result: Hippocampome.org runs on current versions of Chrome, Safari, and Edge browsers, deployed on a CentOS server running Apache. The website runs on PHP from a MySQL database. The code for v2.0 is available open source at GitHub.
evaluation: Claims C100-C103 provide technical specifications. These are direct statements about the implementation. Open source availability (C103) is supported by citation to Wheeler et al., 2023 and enhances reproducibility and community engagement.

result: The Hippocampome.org classification framework defines neuron types based on neurotransmitter and morphological distribution across 26 layers in 6 hippocampal subregions. Two neurons releasing the same neurotransmitter are different types if axons or dendrites of only one invade any layer. Neurons of the same type share the same potential inputs, outputs, and excitatory vs. inhibitory function.
evaluation: Claims C104-C106 describe the fundamental classification framework. These are clearly stated principles illustrated in Figure 1. The framework is logical and provides an objective basis for neuron type definition. This is foundational to the entire resource.

result: The largest increases in pieces of knowledge and evidence in Hippocampome.org were related to synaptic properties. Data underlying synaptic physiology and connection probabilities were supported by over 23,000 pieces of evidence and yielded 500,000 pieces of knowledge through normalized collection of signaling and short-term plasticity parameters for multiple experimental conditions.
evaluation: Claims C109-C110 quantify the data accumulation for synaptic properties. The claims are supported by citations (Moradi and Ascoli, 2020; Tecuatl et al., 2021b; Moradi et al., 2022) and illustrated in Figure 4A. The large number of pieces of knowledge relative to evidence reflects the normalization across multiple experimental conditions described in C21, C41.

result: All freely downloadable model parameters in Hippocampome.org are directly linked to peer-reviewed empirical evidence. Possible research applications include quantitative, multiscale analyses of circuit connectivity and spiking neural network simulations of activity dynamics.
evaluation: Claims C4-C5 state key features and applications. C4 describes a fundamental design principle demonstrated throughout the manuscript. C5 describes potential applications that are demonstrated by the examples in C52-C56 and supported by the framework described in C35-C41. These claims accurately represent the resource's capabilities.
